title: My family
goal: Attach possession to the end of a noun, name the members of your family, and say how old you are.
bekal: form *evim, evin, evi, evimiz, eviniz, evleri* without looking at the table
link two nouns with the pattern *Ayşe'nin evi* — owner first, then the thing owned
ask and give ages with *kaç yaşındasın*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Aile fotoğrafı
dialogs.intro: Fatma Hanım, the landlady, knocks on the door with a tray of tea. There's a family photo on Budi's desk.

lines.speaker: Fatma:
lines.text: Budi, çayın hazır. Bu fotoğraf kimin?
lines.id: Budi, your tea's ready. Whose photo is this?
lines.literal: Budi, tea-your ready. this photo whose?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes, my mother. The one next to her is my father.

lines.speaker: Fatma:
lines.id: Do you have brothers or sisters?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Evet, bir ablam ve bir erkek kardeşim var.
lines.id: Yes, I have an older sister and a younger brother.
lines.literal: yes, one big-sister-my and one male sibling-my there-is.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Yirmi yedi yaşında. Evli, bir kızı var.
lines.id: Twenty-seven. She's married and has a daughter.
lines.literal: twenty seven age-her-at. married, one daughter-her there-is.

lines.speaker: Fatma:
lines.text: Yani sen dayısın! Peki sen kaç yaşındasın?
lines.id: So you're an uncle! And how old are you?
lines.literal: so you uncle-you-are! well you how-many age-at-you-are?

lines.speaker: Fatma:
lines.text: Benim oğlum da senin yaşında. Adı Emre.
lines.id: My son is your age too. His name is Emre.
lines.literal: my son-my too your age-at. name-his Emre.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Is your family big, Aunt Fatma?

lines.speaker: Fatma:
lines.text: Çok büyük! Beş çocuk, on iki torun.
lines.id: Very big! Five children, twelve grandchildren.
lines.literal: very big! five child, ten two grandchild.

notes: **Possession is marked twice — and that's normal.** *Benim ailem* uses *benim* ("my") AND the ending *-m* on *aile*. The ending is required; the word *benim* can be dropped. You use it only for emphasis: "MY family, not someone else's".
**Kaç yaşında literally means "at what age".** Turkish treats age as a place, not a quantity: *yirmi bir yaşındayım* = "I am at age twenty-one". That's why there's a *-da* in the middle.

**Kardeş doesn't say whether it's a brother or a sister.** It means "sibling", male or female. To be specific: *erkek kardeş* (brother), *kız kardeş* (sister). For older siblings a completely different word is used: *abi* and *abla*.

**Dayı and amca are two different words.** *Amca* is your FATHER's brother, *dayı* your MOTHER's brother. Likewise *hala* (father's sister) and *teyze* (mother's sister). Turkish distinguishes family lines that English lumps together as "uncle" and "aunt".

blocks.text: Just like "am/is/are", possession isn't a separate word but an ending. Its form follows four-form vowel harmony, and it adds a linking letter if the host word ends in a vowel.
Look at the third row: words ending in a vowel use the linking letter **s** — *araba-s-ı*, *anne-s-i*, *kapı-s-ı*. This is the second of the three linking letters promised in Unit 1.
If a word ends in **p, ç, t, k** and the ending starts with a vowel, that consonant softens to **b, c, d, ğ**. This isn't an exception but a rule that runs through the whole language:

blocks.title: Why this rule matters right now
items: This softening works for ALL endings that start with a vowel, not just possessives: *kitabı* (his book), *kitaba* (to the book), *sokağa* (to the street), *ağacın* (the tree's).
If you say *kitapım*, people will still understand — but a Turkish ear instantly hears a foreign accent. Softening is one of the cheapest fixes for sounding natural.

blocks.text: To say "Ayşe's house" or "the door of the room", Turkish uses a pattern you'll need to look at twice before it makes sense: **owner + ending -in, then the thing owned + ending -i**. Both are marked.

There's a second, looser pattern: if the owner isn't a specific person or thing but a **type**, the *-in* ending is dropped and only the second word is marked. *Türk kahvesi* (Turkish coffee), *öğrenci yurdu* (student dorm), *ders kitabı* (textbook), *domates çorbası* (tomato soup). You'll see this pattern on every menu.

blocks.title: The apostrophe on proper names
items: Endings attached to **names of people, cities or countries** are separated by an apostrophe: *Ayşe'nin*, *İstanbul'da*, *Türkiye'ye*, *Jakarta'dan*.
This spelling rule is official and used in all writing, WhatsApp messages included. Without the apostrophe, your writing looks like you never finished school.

blocks.text: *Oğul* changes shape once it gets an ending: *oğlum*, *oğlun*, *oğlu* — the *u* in the second syllable drops out. A few short words behave like this: *burun → burnum* (my nose), *şehir → şehri* (its city), *akıl → aklım* (my mind).

blocks.title: Unit 2 review
items: Cover the Turkish and rebuild it from memory: "What's this?" · "These are books and notebooks." · "Who's that?" · "The room is very nice." · "Where's the key?"
Then one harder extra: give the plurals of *sokak*, *öğretmen*, *kapı* and *göz* without looking.

exercises.prompt: Link the two nouns with the *-in ... -i* pattern.

items: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: evim — kitabım — arabam — annem — oğlum — sokağım
Ayşe'nin evi — Budi'nin kitabı — odanın kapısı — öğretmenin arabası — Türkiye'nin başkenti — kardeşimin adı
Bu benim annem. — Kardeşin var mı? — Bir ablam var. — Kaç yaşındasın? — Yirmi bir yaşındayım. — Kardeşim on yaşında.
Bu benim ailem. — Kardeşin var mı? — Yirmi bir yaşındayım. — Ayşe'nin evi çok güzel. — Bu fotoğraf kimin? — Ablan kaç yaşında?
